turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we're late. The parking garage ate my ticket and then the elevator smelled like, I don't know, old coffee.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't worry about it. I'm Dr. Ellison. What got you in this morning?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I got this awful pain in my side. Came on in the night. I don't know, doctor, I've never felt anything like it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Point to it for me. Does it stay there or travel?
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): Left side, kind of the loin, in the back. Then it shoots into my groin. It comes in waves.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): About what time did the waves start?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Two, three in the morning? I don't know, doctor. I wasn't looking at a clock.
[SEG0008] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was 2:40. He was pacing and I looked.
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright, 2:40. I also threw up, just once, in the bathroom.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Once only. Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. It came out pink and then straight red. That's the part that freaked me out.
[SEG0012] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I saw the bowl. It was red, Marcus, not a trick of the light.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): So I'm hearing left loin pain from about 2:40, down to the groin, in waves, one vomit, and red urine. Did I miss a piece?
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): If ten is the worst pain you can picture, where were you?
[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm, a seven or an eight, since about 2:40. I don't know, doctor. The top of the wave is insane and then it backs off a bit.
[SEG0016] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry, vitals. Blood pressure is 148 over 92, heart rate 104, temperature 37.2 celsius, oxygen sat 98 percent, respirations 18.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Burning when you pee?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Diarrhea at all?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Uh, stool's been normal.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or trouble getting a breath?
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): No. None of that.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did you feel feverish, or have chills?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I don't think so.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any surgery in the past?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): Nope. Nothing.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had this kind of pain before, or a known stone?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, something like it. Last winter, or the one before. I don't know, doctor. It quit after a day or two and I never came in.
[SEG0029] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And his father had kidney stones. Twice. He brings it up every time his back acts up.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Yeah. My dad. I don't know any more than that.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): What did you take overnight?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Two tylenol. I don't know the milligrams, doctor.
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Extra strength. 500 each.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Right, so a thousand milligrams by mouth, around four. Just the once.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything you swallow every day?
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I'm not on anything.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies?
[SEG0038] person_3 (PATIENT): Penicillin. Hives, the itchy kind, all over. I'm sure about that one.
[SEG0039] person_4 (NURSE): Urine dip, reading it off. Large blood, three plus. Leukocytes negative. Nitrite negative. Specific gravity 1.015.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Left flank is markedly tender over the kidney. Belly is soft and there's no guarding.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Ow. Yeah. Hey, wait, I messed up the fever thing. Around midnight I was burning up, sweat through my t-shirt, like a real fever. I don't have a number, I didn't check.
[SEG0042] person_4 (NURSE): My sister had a stone last spring. Told everybody it beat childbirth. That's her story, not yours, I just thought of her when I saw you hunched over.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): The picture fits a stone sitting in the ureter. The ureter spasms around it, so the pain rolls in waves toward the groin, and the stone scratches the lining, so you bleed. The dip has blood and no markers of infection. Working idea only, the pictures still have to back it up.
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): So my kidney's okay? I don't know, doctor.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): A lot of these pass on their own. For the pain I'm giving ketoralac, 30 milligrams into the muscle, once, right now. And tamsolosin, 0.4 milligrams by mouth, once a day, so the ureter eases up.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Jen will draw blood this morning before you leave, a blood count and a creatinine. You don't need to fast. Just stay put until the tubes are done.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I've booked a non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis for today at two. Drink a little water and check in at radiology at two.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): If that CT is borderline and we still can't see the stone, then we do an ultrasound. I'm not scheduling that unless the CT is borderline.

[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in two weeks. Try to get about two liters of fluid in today if it stays down, and strain your urine. If you can't keep fluids down or the pain takes off again, go to the ER.
[SEG0050] person_4 (NURSE): I'll be right in with the shot and the tubes.

spec.situation: Sudden severe loin pain going to the groin overnight, vomiting once, blood in urine; pain score given loosely; urine dip result read aloud; painkiller and scan planned today.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
